Impact of Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi on Lactuca sativa 
Growth in Lunar Simulant Soil 
 
Alyson Lang, Vivian Luo 
Mycorrhizal Moon – #23562 
Eastside Preparatory School 
Plant The Moon Challenge, Fall 2025, High School Division

1 
 
BACKGROUND 
Arbuscular mycorrhizal (AM) fungi form one of the most ancient and widespread 
plant–microbe symbioses, occurring in the roots of the majority of land plants (Chen et al., 
2018). Through this mutualistic association, AM fungi provide crucial benefits to their host 
plants by enhancing nutrient acquisition (especially phosphorus and nitrogen) and water uptake, 
while also improving plant stress tolerance (Chen et al., 2018). In exchange, the plant supplies 
the fungus with carbohydrates, allocating up to ~20% of its photosynthetically fixed carbon to 
support the fungus The net effect of this partnership is often increased plant growth and biomass 
production under nutrient-limited conditions, as the fungi’s hyphal networks access nutrients 
beyond the root’s immediate reach. Given the extreme nutrient poverty and abrasive, inert nature 
of lunar regolith, harnessing AM fungal symbioses has astrobiological appeal: it could help 
plants acquire scarce nutrients and reduce the need for heavy fertilizer inputs in extraterrestrial 
agriculture. Researchers have begun exploring such approaches in space analog soils, with 
evidence that AM fungi can improve plant performance even in simulants of lunar soil by 
boosting nutrient uptake and mitigating substrate toxicity (Parniske, M. 2008). This experiment 
builds on that rationale, investigating whether AM fungal inoculation can facilitate lettuce 
(Lactuca sativa) growth in a lunar regolith simulant by creating a more supportive, 
nutrient-accessible rhizosphere. 
 
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN 
The plants were grown in a cabinet at Eastside Preparatory School lit by a white LED 
light bar. The cabinet allowed air flow with the room-temperature classroom outside but blocked 
nearly all light coming from that room. So, constants such as light, temperature, and air content 
were easily maintained. Watering and measuring the plants left the cabinet doors open for about 
1 hour every week, a disturbance that was deemed negligible. 
The growth medium consisted of a mixture of 50% lunar regolith simulant (LHS-1), 
27.5% fine sand to reduce compaction, 7.5% perlite for aeration and drainage, 5% compost to 
provide minimal nutrients that make fungal benefits measurable, and 10% fungal inoculant. This 
mixture balanced biological realism (low nutrients, simulating lunar soil) with the minimum

2 
 
conditions necessary for plant survival. The fungal inoculant (Endo Blend Granular Mycorrhizal 
Inoculant from The Soil Makers) was chosen because it had four different strains of AM fungi 
and was free of other additives. These fungi have a synergistic effect on each other which 
quickens inoculation, and a larger number of AM fungi strains increases the likelihood that one 
strain will be a more suitable symbiotic partner for the lettuce (Chen et al., 2018). The dormant 
fungal spores are carried by mineral clay fragments which, though inert, is still an extra variable 
that must be controlled. So, instead of only adding inoculant to the experimental group, half of 
the inoculant was sterilized before being added to the control group as well. The sand, perlite, 
and compost were also sterilized to minimize the chances of introducing unwanted 
microorganisms into the medium. In addition, distilled water was used to water the plants so that 
none of the minerals and contamination present in tap water (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, nitrates, 
organic compounds, etc.) would enrich the low-nutrient soil. 
Measurements taken weekly from weeks 1-7 to gauge overall plant health included plant 
height, width, leaf count, and qualitative changes documented through standardized photographs 
with scale references. At week 8, one plant per pot was harvested and analyzed for root length, 
fresh and dry biomass of shoots and roots, and fungal colonization levels. This data is most 
useful for answering our question but could not be recorded before the end of the grow period 
without causing significant plant stress and root breakage. 
 
HYPOTHESIS 
We hypothesized that lettuce plants grown in a nutrient-poor lunar regolith simulant 
would show improved growth and survival when inoculated with AM fungi, compared to 
uninoculated control plants. In particular, the presence of live AM fungi was expected to enhance 
the host’s uptake of phosphorus and nitrogen from the simulant, thereby increasing plant biomass 
accumulation and health relative to non-mycorrhizal controls. 
 
INDEPENDENT VARIABLES

3 
 
The primary independent variable in this experiment was the presence versus absence of 
live AM fungal inoculation in the growth medium. The experimental group (“+AMF”) received a 
Glomus-based AM fungal inoculum mixed into the potting substrate, whereas the control group 
(“–AMF”) was given the same substrate mixture but with the inoculum sterilized to eliminate 
any viable fungi. In practice, both groups used an identical soil blend but only the experimental 
pots contained live mycorrhizal fungi. Thus, any differences in plant growth between treatments 
can be attributed to the effect of the AM fungi introduced in experimental conditions. 
 
DEPENDENT VARIABLES 
Plant growth and health were tracked through multiple dependent variables, 
encompassing both quantitative morphology measures and symbiotic indicators. Throughout the 
8-week growth period, we recorded above-ground growth metrics such as seedling emergence 
rate, plant height, rosette diameter (leaf spread), number of leaves per plant, and the area of the 
largest leaf. These metrics reflected overall vigor and canopy development. At harvest, below- 
ground traits were assessed, and the p-values determined through the Student’s t-test: we 
measured the length of the longest root and the total root biomass (fresh weight and dry weight) 
for each plant, alongside shoot biomass, to evaluate how the treatments affected root 
development and total productivity. Additionally, to confirm and quantify the symbiosis in the 
inoculated group, we determined the percentage of root length colonized by AM fungi via 
microscopic examination of cleared and stained root samples. This suite of dependent variables 
enabled a comprehensive comparison of plant performance (in both shoots and roots) and fungal 
colonization between mycorrhizal and non-mycorrhizal treatments. 
 
CONTROLS 
Several environmental and substrate factors were rigorously controlled to ensure that the 
two treatment groups experienced identical conditions aside from the mycorrhizal inoculum. All 
pots were prepared with the same base soil composition, mixed in a single batch to homogenize 
nutrients and texture. Each pot was given an equal soil volume and initially received the same

4 
 
batch of lettuce seeds to standardize germination potential. Light conditions were uniform: plants 
were grown under white LED lamps on a 14-hour light/10-hour dark cycle, simulating a 
consistent diurnal rhythm for photosynthesis. Temperature and relative humidity were 
maintained at stable growth-chamber settings (approximately 21–23°C and ~50% humidity) for 
all pots. We also controlled the watering schedule across treatments – for example, in early 
weeks all plants were misted daily, and in later weeks each pot received the same measured 
volumes of water on the same days, with adjustments made in unison as plants grew. Soil pH 
was monitored weekly and remained around neutral (pH ~7.0) in both groups, a level optimal for 
lettuce growth and AM fungal activity. To prevent any cross-contamination of live fungi into 
control pots, physical precautions were in place: each pot’s drainage was isolated (pots were 
elevated above catch trays so that leachate couldn’t flow between them), and husbandry tools 
were sterilized between use on control vs. experimental groups. These controls ensured that any 
observed differences in plant growth could be attributed to the presence of AM fungi rather than 
extraneous variables. 
 
METHODS 
A substrate mixture consisting of 1.1 kg fine sand, 300 g perlite, 200 g compost, and 200 
g fungal inoculant was sterilized in a pressure cooker on steam mode for 60 min at 15 psi, using 
1.3 cups of water placed outside the Mason jars containing the substrate. The sterilized sand, 
perlite, and compost were then mixed with 2.0 kg LHS-1 and approximately 500 mL deionized 
water. Next, 185 g of unsterilized inoculant was mixed into half of the soil mixture, and 185 g of 
sterilized inoculant was mixed into the remaining half. 
Eighteen pots were labeled as control (C) or experimental (E) and numbered 1–9 within 
each group. For record-keeping, individual plants within each pot were later labeled 1–15 from 
the top left to the bottom right corner after a dash (e.g., C9-15). Thin cloth was placed over the 
drainage holes to minimize substrate loss, and each pot was elevated approximately 1 cm from 
the container bottom to prevent drained water from mixing between pots and contaminating the 
control group with live fungi. All pots were filled with equal amounts of the substrate mixture. 
Approximately 1.6 g sterilized inoculant was added to each of the nine control pots, and ~1.6 g

5 
 
unsterilized inoculant was added to each of the nine experimental pots, ensuring placement that 
promoted root contact. 
Approximately 500 lettuce grains were germinated by soaking, rinsing, and placing them 
on a damp towel. The 270 healthiest seedlings were selected, and 15 seedlings were positioned 
equidistantly in each of the 18 pots. All pots were placed in a dark cabinet approximately 0.5 m 
below white LED lights programmed for 14h daylight and 10h night. Watering was adjusted as 
plants developed: daily misting during the first two weeks, 20 mL every other day during weeks 
3–4, and gradually increasing volumes during weeks 5–8. Watering amounts were changed if 
plant showed signs of overwatering or underwatering, but the two groups always got the same 
amount and frequency of water. When the space became limited or the lettuce became too 
entangled, a constant number of the smallest plants from each pot were thinned out and disposed. 
Once a week during weeks 1-7, the healthiest plant in each pot was measured. Its height 
was recorded as the length of its primary stem, and its width as the added length of its two 
longest lateral stems. Leaf count was the number of live leaves. Then, a top-down photograph of 
all plants was taken with the control group on the left and the experimental group on the right, 
and a 30cm ruler for reference. 
At week 8, all plants were harvested. First, plants and soil were removed from the pots, 
and plant roots were rinsed clean of soil. The healthiest plant from each pot was kept and the rest 
discarded. After drying and separating the roots and shoots of each plant, the wet biomass of 
roots and shoots were then weighed. Plant material was then cut into ~1 cm pieces. The pieces 
were mixed, and a subsample of each plant was put into each of 18 Eppendorf tubes for storage. 
With the use of PPE, 1 mL KOH was added to each tube to clear and preserve the tissue. Then, 
tubes were closed and placed on a rack for later dyeing and microscopy. 
The remaining root pieces were weighed again to get the partial wet root biomass. These 
roots were then placed into a second set of Eppendorf tubes and left with open caps in a dry, 
warm cabinet for one week. Dry biomass of whole roots was extrapolated from percent weight 
change in the partial biomass. Shoots were dried between sheets of paper in a heavy notebook. 
After a week, the dry shoot biomass was recorded.

6 
 
Then, the staining procedure was carried out to dye root fungi with ink so they would be 
visible under a compound microscope. Root samples in KOH were incubated in a heat block for 
10 min at 90 °C. Using PPE and a micropipette, KOH was removed then diluted in water to be 
disposed of safely. KOH served to de-stain the roots and degrade cell walls to improve staining 
quality. Afterward, 1 mL of a 5% acetic acid solution, the purest available store-bought white 
vinegar, was added to each tube to wash the roots. After removing the acid, 1 mL staining 
solution (5% Higgins non-waterproof black ink in 95% store-bought vinegar) was added to each 
tube, and samples were heated for 10 min at 90 °C. 
Roots were removed with tweezers, rinsed with water, and transferred to microscope 
slides containing glycerol as a mounting medium. Coverslips were applied and sealed with nail 
polish. Prepared samples were examined under a microscope to visualize stained fungal 
structures, and rough percent colonization was recorded (Jarratt-Barnham, 2024). 
 
RESULTS 
​
While on most weeks the lettuce were regularly watered on Mondays, Wednesdays, and 
Fridays, holidays and other school closures interrupted that schedule, and some waterings were 
skipped for fear of overwatering. The plants were thinned to 5 per pot after week 2, 3 per pot at 
week 5, and 1 per pot after harvesting at week 8. Further observations, dates, and watering 
details from the grow period are available in Appendix S1. Raw data for the following 
post-growth analysis graphs can be found in Appendix S2.

7 
 
 
​
 
In Figures 3-6, data points represent average values, and error bars represent standard 
deviation. Data on lettuce width over time can be found in both appendices but was omitted from 
this report because of unreliable measurements: sometimes, lateral leaves were not extended 
before being measured, so as a result, those measurements were largely determined by leaf 
limpness instead of leaf length.

Through microscopy, we found that Higgins ink did not stain any root structures, and no 
fungi were visible (Fig. 7). So, the staining and microscopy procedures were attempted again 
using Sheaffer ink, which had been successful in similar experiments (Jarratt-Barnham, 2024). 
However, many of the roots became too dark, and there was no obvious sign of fungi (Fig. 8). 
Additionally, since the same roots were reused in the second attempt, they had sustained damage 
from handling and were not as well preserved as before.

9 
 
 
Fig. 7. Microscopy of root samples from each plant, dyed with Higgins non-waterproof black 
ink. No fungi were visible in any of the samples. 
 
 
Fig. 8. Microscopy of root samples from each plant, dyed with Sheaffer black ink. The C2 
sample was lost during staining. No fungi were visible in any of the samples. 
 
 
DISCUSSION & CONCLUSIONS 
We were unable to confirm fungal colonization via microscopy in the experimental 
group, but this absence does not conclusively mean the symbiosis failed. Root damage and 
imperfect dye strength could have interfered with the visibility of fungi, and additional abiotic 
stressors, such as erratic humidity or suboptimal temperatures, could have further hindered 
colonization or fungal survival. Moreover, the inoculum viability may have been compromised,

10 
 
or native pathogens may have outcompeted the introduced fungi. Only a subset of roots was 
sampled for staining and microscopic observation, leaving the possibility that colonized 
segments were missed, especially if colonization was sparse or uneven. AM symbiosis typically 
takes several weeks to establish, and more for the fungi to expand. With more time, qPCR or 
AMScorer and AMReader could be used to confirm the presence and quantity of fungi 
(Jaratt-Barnham, 2024). Still, the consistent and statistically significant differences in biomass 
and root morphology between treatments suggest that AM fungi or at least their attempted 
establishment had measurable physiological effects. This validates the experiment's core inquiry 
and highlights the critical role of timing, fungal compatibility, and environmental control in the 
success of plant–microbe partnerships in extraterrestrial agriculture. 
Contrary to our initial expectations, the AM fungi inoculation did not dramatically 
improve lettuce growth in the lunar regolith simulant. By the end of the trial, there were no 
significant increases in shoot biomass or leaf production attributable to the mycorrhiza; instead, 
the control group (no AM fungi) developed longer average root lengths and greater dry biomass 
than the mycorrhizal group, a difference that was statistically significant (p < 0.01). One 
interpretation is that non-inoculated plants, facing nutrient scarcity alone, responded by investing 
more into root exploration, thereby growing longer roots in search of nutrients. In contrast, 
mycorrhiza-inoculated plants may have allocated resources differently – perhaps relying more on 
the fungus for nutrient foraging instead of extending roots, or conversely, being hampered in root 
growth by the metabolic costs of supporting the fungus. The similar (or lower) shoot and leaf 
yields in the inoculated plants suggest that the anticipated benefits of the symbiosis (improved 
nutrient uptake leading to greater biomass) did not fully materialize under these conditions. 
Several biological factors could explain why the AM fungi failed to confer a growth 
advantage in the harsh, low-nutrient simulant, and why inoculated plants had less growth than 
controls. Functional specificity is one important consideration: not all AM fungi species are 
equally beneficial to all host plants, especially under extreme nutrient stress. It is known from 
other studies that mycorrhizal growth responses can vary from highly positive to neutral or even 
negative depending on the particular fungal strain and the soil nutrient context (Wang et al., 
2016). The commercial inoculum used contained species of Rhizophagus/Glomus that have been 
effective in crops including lettuce, but it’s possible that in Lactuca sativa and under the

11 
 
near-starvation phosphorus levels of the simulant, the symbiosis was suboptimal. Indeed, prior 
research on legumes has shown that only certain AM fungal partners significantly improved 
growth at low phosphorus, while others provided little to no benefit (Wang et al., 2016). If the 
dominant fungi in our inoculum were not functionally well-matched to scavenging phosphorus in 
regolith or to associating with lettuce roots, the plants might not have received a net nutrient 
boost despite being colonized. 
Another likely factor is the carbon cost of supporting the fungi under conditions of severe 
nutrient limitation. While AM fungi can enhance a plant’s access to nutrients, the symbiosis is 
not free – the plant must pay a substantial carbon fee to its fungal partners. Parniske (2008) noted 
that up to 20% of a host’s photosynthates can be shunted to the fungus (Andrino et al., 2020). In 
a nutrient-poor environment, a plant’s energy and carbon resources are already limited; allocating 
a large fraction of its photosynthetic output to the fungus could become detrimental if the fungus 
cannot supply adequate nutrients in return. The literature suggests that under extremely low soil 
fertility, the trade balance of the symbiosis can tip unfavorably for the plant: as soil phosphorus 
becomes less available, plants actually have to invest even more carbon to maintain the fungal 
network, due to the fungus needing to grow more extensively and respire more to find scarce 
nutrients (Andrino et al., 2020). Our experimental conditions – essentially a sand/regolith 
mixture with minimal available P or N – may have exemplified this scenario. It is possible that 
the fungi simply could not scavenge enough phosphorus from the simulant to repay the plant in 
kind. This outcome aligns with the concept that AM fungi can behave as carbon sinks or even 
mild parasites when nutrients are too scarce to fuel a mutualistic exchange (Andrino et al., 2020). 
It is also plausible that biotic interactions or stress responses interfered with the expected 
mycorrhizal benefits. The introduction of live inoculum, despite efforts at purity, could have 
brought in other soil microorganisms (such as saprophytic fungi or bacteria) or latent pathogens. 
In a closed pot system with very limited nutrients, any introduced microbe could compete with 
the plants for those nutrients or otherwise impact root health. If, for instance, some microbial 
contaminants proliferated in the experimental pots, they might have negated the positive effects 
of the AM fungi or even caused additional stress to the plants (damping-off, minor root rot, etc.), 
thereby suppressing growth. Even the AM fungi themselves could induce a mild defense 
response in lettuce under these novel conditions – plants that are heavily colonized sometimes

12 
 
exhibit growth depressions if the symbiosis functionality is imbalanced. Additionally, the sterile 
starting conditions mean the native soil microbiome (which can assist plant growth) was absent; 
the control plants, though lacking AMF, also lacked any microbes, whereas the experimental 
plants had AMF but not necessarily the full complement of helpful rhizobacteria that often co-act 
with mycorrhizae. In natural settings, mycorrhizal fungi often work in concert with certain 
bacteria, a synergy which would be missing here. 
An alternative explanation for the absence of visible AM fungal structures in stained 
roots is that the commercial inoculum may not have contained viable fungal propagules capable 
of establishing a symbiosis. A recent systematic evaluation of 16 commercially marketed AM 
fungal inoculants found that only three products actually led to measurable root colonization, and 
only one conferred a positive growth response under controlled greenhouse conditions (i.e., 
increased biomass relative to uninoculated controls) (Boussageon et al., 2025). Furthermore, an 
expanded analysis across dozens of global products revealed that the vast majority of 
commercial AMF inoculants fail to induce colonization in plant roots, with up to 85 % of tested 
products showing poor quality and no measurable symbiotic effect (Boussageon et al., 2025). 
This suggests that many commercial preparations may be marketed as “mycorrhizal” without 
actually delivering live, viable fungi in sufficient propagule numbers. In our experiment, if the 
inoculum lacked sufficient viable AM fungal spores or hyphae, then inoculated plants would not 
have established a true symbiotic network, explaining both the lack of symbiotic structures seen 
under microscopy and the lower biomass in the experimental group. 
Moreover, commercial products may contain abiotic or non-fungal components (such as 
nutrient carriers, organic material, or mineral supplements) that can promote plant growth in 
nutrient-rich garden soils but do not function as true mycorrhizal inoculants in extreme, 
low-nutrient substrates like lunar regolith simulant. Some analyses indicate that perceived 
benefits from such products in horticultural contexts could stem from these additives rather than 
genuine fungal activity, as many inoculants rely on nutrient fertilizers or biostimulant carriers to 
give an appearance of effectiveness in conventional settings but fail to establish functional 
fungal–plant symbioses in rigorous tests (e.g., root colonization assays). In our context, the 
presence of non-fungal growth stimulants would not substitute for the nutrient acquisition role 
normally provided by AM fungi, especially in an oligotrophic substrate with minimal organic

13 
 
matter. If the inoculum primarily contributed abiotic growth aids rather than viable fungi, any 
observed effects (or lack thereof) would be misattributed to mycorrhizal activity, confounding 
interpretation. These considerations underscore that commercial AMF products should be 
independently verified for propagule viability and colonization potential before deployment in 
research or extraterrestrial agriculture applications, since a failure to establish living mycorrhizal 
networks can lead to misleading experimental outcomes and incorrect conclusions about the role 
and utility of AM fungi in novel environments. 
In summary, this astrobiology-inspired experiment demonstrated that simply inoculating 
lettuce with AM fungi in a lunar regolith simulant did not automatically yield better growth, 
underscoring the nuanced, context-dependent nature of mycorrhizal symbiosis. Our hypothesis 
that AM fungi would markedly improve plant performance in the simulant was not supported by 
the final results. These findings highlight that while AM fungi are globally beneficial mutualists, 
their efficacy in unconventional substrates (like lunar soil analogs) hinges on multiple factors: 
the right fungal partner, the presence of at least minimal accessible nutrients, and a favorable 
balance between costs and benefits to the host. For future research aimed at space agriculture, 
this suggests that additional strategies may be required to unlock the value of AM fungi. For 
example, selecting more efficient fungal strains (those functionally specialized for nutrient 
scavenging under extreme P starvation), co-inoculating with growth-promoting bacteria, or 
slightly amending the regolith with nutrients to support the fungus could all potentially tip the 
balance toward a beneficial outcome. The concept of using AM fungi to facilitate plant growth in 
lunar regolith remains promising in principle, but our results emphasize that the implementation 
must account for the complex biological and environmental interactions at play. The functional 
specificity of the plant–fungus pairing, the carbon trade economy of the symbiosis, and the 
extreme nutrient context all determine whether AM fungi act as helpers or hindrances in a given 
scenario (Wang et al., 2016). Understanding and optimizing these factors will be crucial as we 
continue to explore sustainable methods for cultivating food crops beyond Earth.
